423	// decodeConfigRoutes is check layer 2: the top-level object is taken apart
424	// and every route entry is type-checked against its 1-based position. The
425	// routes field must hold an array when present — null is a type error here,
426	// never an absent field: a config that explicitly supplies routes must supply
427	// an array. A non-object entry (null included) fails on that entry before
428	// any field is inspected, and a wrong field type is reported on the offending
429	// route with its id when the route supplies a valid non-empty string id
430	// anywhere in its object. Each route's unchecked queryTransforms value
431	// travels in the returned pendingRoutes for layer 3.
432	func decodeConfigRoutes(body json.RawMessage) ([]pendingRoute, error) {
433		var fields map[string]json.RawMessage
434		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &fields); err != nil {
435			return nil, err
436		}
437	
438		var rawRoutes []json.RawMessage
439		if raw, ok := fields["routes"]; ok {
440			elem := bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
441			if len(elem) == 0 || elem[0] != '[' {
442				return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "routes must be an array, got %s", jsonTypeName(elem))
443			}
444			if err := json.Unmarshal(elem, &rawRoutes); err != nil {
445				return nil, err
446			}
447		}
448	
449		routes := make([]pendingRoute, len(rawRoutes))
450		for i, entry := range rawRoutes {
451			route, f := decodeRoute(entry, fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1))
452			if f != nil {
453				return nil, f
454			}
455			routes[i] = route
456		}
457		return routes, nil
458	}

460	// checkQueryTransforms is check layer 3: every route's raw queryTransforms
461	// value is decoded and validated against the route's 1-based position, in
462	// routes-array order, and the validated rules replace the pending raw value.
463	// It runs only after layer 2 has cleared every route, so a basic-field type
464	// error on any route — earlier or later — is always reported before any rule
465	// error, while within this layer the earliest route (and within it the
466	// earliest rule) wins.
467	func checkQueryTransforms(routes []pendingRoute) *Failure {
468		for i := range routes {
469			if len(routes[i].rawTransforms) == 0 {
470				continue // field absent
471			}
472			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
473			transforms, f := parseQueryTransforms(routes[i].rawTransforms, loc, routes[i].route.ID)
474			if f != nil {
475				return f
476			}
477			routes[i].route.QueryTransforms = transforms
478			routes[i].rawTransforms = nil
479		}
480		return nil
481	}

485	// judging its shape. It returns encoding/json's own error verbatim, so each
486	// caller keeps its existing handling (ParseConfig wraps a returned error just
487	// as Config.UnmarshalJSON returning it directly always has).
488	func unmarshalJSONValue(data []byte) (json.RawMessage, error) {

497	// legal value that is not a JSON object is a structural error in the caller's
498	// code saying "<what> must be a JSON object", never a parse failure and never

500	// actually received ("got <type>"); the request wording omits it.

503			if nameType {
504				return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object, got %s", what, jsonTypeName(doc))
505			}
506			return failuref(code, "%s must be a JSON object", what)
507		}
508		return nil
509	}

537	// ParseConfig parses and fully validates the route configuration. Reading
538	// checks the document in four layers, and the first layer that finds a
539	// problem decides which error is reported:
540	//
541	//  1. JSON syntax: a broken document is only ever a parse failure, reported
542	//     without a guessed route position or field.
543	//  2. Structure and basic field types: the top-level value must be an
544	//     object, routes must be an array of objects, and id, methods,
545	//     pathPrefix and upstream must carry their JSON types.
546	//  3. Query rewrite rules: each route's queryTransforms array and every rule
547	//     in it.
548	//  4. Field contents: a non-empty unique id, legal methods, an absolute
549	//     pathPrefix (with no direct space, C0 control byte or DEL — only
550	//     percent encoding may carry those) and a valid upstream
551	//     (Config.validate).
552	//
553	// Within one layer the earliest array position wins — routes by their
554	// position in the routes array and rules by their position in the route's
555	// queryTransforms array, never by id ordering or by the object field order.
556	// Layers 1–3 run in Config.UnmarshalJSON (so they also guard a plain
557	// json.Unmarshal into a Config); layer 4 runs here, after decoding. Every
558	// failure hands back no config at all, so a half-parsed configuration can
559	// never resolve a request.
560	func ParseConfig(data []byte) (*Config, *Failure) {
561		var cfg Config
562		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &cfg); err != nil {
563			if f, ok := err.(*Failure); ok {
564				return nil, f
565			}
566			return nil, failuref("invalid_config", "config is not valid JSON: %v", err)
567		}
568		if f := cfg.validate(); f != nil {
569			return nil, f
570		}
571		return &cfg, nil
572	}
573	
574	// validate is check layer 4 (see ParseConfig): the field contents of every
575	// route, in routes-array order. It runs only after layers 1–3 have cleared
576	// the whole document, so any structure, field-type or rule error anywhere is
577	// reported before any content error.
578	func (cfg *Config) validate() *Failure {
579		seenIDs := make(map[string]int, len(cfg.Routes))
580		for i := range cfg.Routes {
581			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
582			loc := fmt.Sprintf("route %d", i+1)
583			if route.ID == "" {
584				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: id must be non-empty", loc)
585			}
586			if first, ok := seenIDs[route.ID]; ok {
587				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s: duplicate id %q (already used by route %d)", loc, route.ID, first)
588			}
589			seenIDs[route.ID] = i + 1
590	
591			if len(route.Methods) == 0 {
592				return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must be a non-empty array", loc, route.ID)
593			}
594			for _, method := range route.Methods {
595				switch {
596				case method == "":
597					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): methods must not contain empty entries", loc, route.ID)
598				case method == "*":
599					// Wildcard matching any legal method.
600				case !isToken(method):
601					return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): invalid method %q", loc, route.ID, method)
602				}
603			}
604	
605			if f := validatePrefix(route.PathPrefix, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
606				return f
607			}
608			if f := validateUpstream(route.Upstream, loc, route.ID); f != nil {
609				return f
610			}
611		}
612		return nil
613	}

615	func validatePrefix(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
616		switch {
617		case prefix == "" || prefix[0] != '/':
618			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must start with /", loc, id)
619		case prefix != "/" && strings.HasSuffix(prefix, "/"):
620			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not end with / except for root", loc, id)
621		case strings.ContainsAny(prefix, "?#"):
622			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
623		case !validPercentEscapes(prefix):
624			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains an invalid percent escape", loc, id)
625		}
626		if f := validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id); f != nil {
627			return f
628		}
629		return nil
630	}
631	
632	// validatePrefixDirectCharacters rejects a direct space or control byte in a
633	// pathPrefix: a direct ASCII space (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000
634	// through U+001F) or DEL (U+007F) makes the whole configuration
635	// invalid_config, because a request target can never carry that character
636	// directly — ParseRequest rejects it before route selection — so such a
637	// prefix could never be hit by a legal request. The check is decided on the
638	// decoded configured string: writing the byte literally or spelling it as a
639	// JSON escape ("\n", "\t", or the backslash-u0020 space escape) decodes to
640	// the same byte and fails
641	// the same way. Bytes inside a well-formed percent escape are skipped
642	// without decoding, so "%20", "%09" and "%00" stay legal raw text and keep
643	// matching on the raw encoded form; the prefix is never trimmed, the byte is
644	// never stripped or percent-encoded on the user's behalf, and the rule is
645	// not widened to other Unicode content (e.g. Chinese characters). It runs in
646	// check layer 4 (Config.validate), after JSON syntax, structure and basic
647	// field types and the queryTransforms rules, in routes-array order like the
648	// other field-content checks, so a later route's bad queryTransforms rule or
649	// an earlier route's other content error keeps its existing precedence. The
650	// reason names the pathPrefix field, the route's 1-based position and valid
651	// non-empty id and the first offending character as U+XXXX.
652	func validatePrefixDirectCharacters(prefix, loc, id string) *Failure {
653		if c, ok := firstDirectRawCharacter(prefix); ok {
654			return failuref("invalid_config",
655				"%s (id %q): pathPrefix contains a character that must be percent-encoded: U+%04X is not allowed to appear directly in a pathPrefix (a request target may not carry it directly either, so no legal request could match this route; percent-encode it, e.g. %%20 for a space; the prefix is used exactly as configured and the byte is never stripped, trimmed or encoded on its behalf)",
656				loc, id, c)
657		}
658		return nil
659	}

661	// upstreamParts is the one shared reading of a raw upstream URL's address
662	// boundaries. Every field is a slice of the original bytes (nothing is
663	// copied, decoded or normalized), so validation and joining cannot disagree
664	// about where one part ends and the next begins:
665	//
666	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] hostPort basePath
667	//
668	// authority runs from after "://" to the first path slash, and hostPort is
669	// the authority after its last '@', so colons in userinfo or the base path
670	// can never be read as part of an IPv6 host, while brackets, a port and a
671	// zone stay inside hostPort.
672	type upstreamParts struct {
673		raw       string // the upstream exactly as configured; every other field slices this
674		schemeEnd int    // index of the ':' in "://", or -1 when the scheme is absent
675		authority string // bytes between "://" and the first path slash (userinfo included)
676		hostPort  string // authority after the last '@' (host plus optional port)
677		basePath  string // from the first path slash to the end, or ""
678	}
679	
680	// splitUpstream applies the single boundary rule shared by the bracketed-host
681	// check, the unbracketed-IPv6 check and the final join. It never rejects
682	// anything on its own: a raw value without "://" comes back with schemeEnd
683	// set to -1 and empty parts, leaving the generic absolute-URL check to
684	// report it, exactly as the per-caller preamble used to.
685	func splitUpstream(raw string) upstreamParts {
686		p := upstreamParts{raw: raw, schemeEnd: -1}
687		i := strings.Index(raw, "://")
688		if i < 0 {
689			return p
690		}
691		p.schemeEnd = i
692		tail := raw[i+3:]
693		if j := strings.IndexByte(tail, '/'); j >= 0 {
694			p.authority = tail[:j]
695			p.basePath = tail[j:]
696		} else {
697			p.authority = tail
698		}
699		// Any userinfo precedes the host and ends at the last '@'; that boundary
700		// is what keeps a userinfo colon out of the IPv6-host checks.
701		p.hostPort = p.authority
702		if k := strings.LastIndexByte(p.authority, '@'); k >= 0 {
703			p.hostPort = p.authority[k+1:]
704		}
705		return p
706	}
707	
708	func validateUpstream(raw, loc, id string) *Failure {
709		if strings.ContainsAny(raw, "?#") {
710			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must not contain a query string or fragment", loc, id)
711		}
712		// Validate the host's IP-literal spelling against the raw string before
713		// url.Parse: square brackets are the IP-literal marker, so whatever they
714		// enclose must be a legal IPv6 address (full, compressed or IPv4-tail,
715		// zone included) rather than a name or an IPv4 address, and an IPv6
716		// literal may never appear without that pair of brackets. Both checks and
717		// the later join read the same splitUpstream boundaries, which keeps the
718		// rules independent of url.Parse's parser strictness and lets the reason
719		// name the field and the actual problem instead of surfacing a generic URL
720		// parse error (an unbracketed literal otherwise reaches the user as a
721		// misleading "invalid port" complaint).
722		p := splitUpstream(raw)
723		if f := validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
724			return f
725		}
726		if f := validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p, loc, id); f != nil {
727			return f
728		}
729		if f := validateUpstreamHostPresent(p, loc, id); f != nil {
730			return f
731		}
732		if f := validateUpstreamPortRange(p, loc, id); f != nil {
733			return f
734		}
735		if f := validateUpstreamBasePathSpace(p, loc, id); f != nil {
736			return f
737		}
738		u, err := url.Parse(raw)
739		if err != nil {
740			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream is not a valid URL: %v", loc, id, err)
741		}
742		if u.Scheme != "http" && u.Scheme != "https" {
743			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must be an absolute http or https URL", loc, id)
744		}
745		if u.Host == "" {
746			return failuref("invalid_config", "%s (id %q): upstream must include a host", loc, id)
747		}
748		return nil
749	}
750	
751	// validateUpstreamHostPresent enforces on the split raw boundaries that the
752	// authority carries a non-empty host:
753	//
754	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] host [":" port] [basePath]
755	//
756	// The check is needed because url.Parse treats a leading colon as a port
757	// separator with an empty hostname: it reads "http://:8080/base" with
758	// Host==":8080" and Hostname()=="" instead of rejecting it, so a check on
759	// u.Host alone lets the address through and the joined upstream is emitted
760	// without a host. The raw decision therefore fails every hostPort that is
761	// empty or begins with the port colon — an empty authority
762	// ("http:///base"), an authority reduced to userinfo ("http://u@/base"),
763	// a bare port with or without digits ("http://:8080/base",
764	// "https://:8443", "http://:/base") and any of those after userinfo
765	// ("https://user:p%40ss@:8443/v1"). Neither userinfo, the port nor a base
766	// path can fill the host slot, no default address is ever substituted, and
767	// a host that is simply followed by an empty port ("http://host:/base")
768	// stays accepted: its hostPort begins with the host, not the separator.
769	// Like the bracket rules this is a content error in a syntactically valid
770	// JSON document — the reason names the route's 1-based position, its id and
771	// the upstream field and says the upstream is missing a host, never that
772	// the JSON is broken or that an IPv6 literal needs brackets.
773	func validateUpstreamHostPresent(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
774		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
775			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
776		}
777		hostPort := p.hostPort
778		if hostPort != "" && hostPort[0] != ':' {
779			return nil
780		}
781		return failuref("invalid_config",
782			"%s: upstream %q is missing a host: the address must carry a non-empty host before any port (e.g. \"http://example.com:8080/base\"); a port cannot serve as the host, and userinfo or a base path cannot fill the host in either; no default host is added",
783			routeLabel(loc, id), p.raw)
784	}
785	
786	// validateUpstreamPortRange enforces the TCP port range on an explicitly
787	// written, non-empty, all-digits port in the upstream address:
788	//
789	//	scheme "://" [userinfo "@"] host [":" port] [basePath]
790	//
791	// A port is a decimal number from 0 to 65535, both ends included; 65536 or
792	// anything larger is not a TCP port and the whole configuration fails as
793	// invalid_config. The decision is made on the decimal value, not the string
794	// length: leading zeros change nothing ("00065535" is legal, "00065536" is
795	// not), and the digit string is compared without ever being converted to an
796	// integer, so a port of arbitrary length cannot overflow a conversion into
797	// an accepted value or crash the read. The comparison is length-then-
798	// lexicographic against "65535" on the zero-stripped digits, which is exact
799	// for equal-length decimal strings.
800	//
801	// The port is sliced out of the same splitUpstream hostPort boundaries the
802	// host validators and the final join use, so only the real port is judged:
803	// the colon inside userinfo ends at the last '@' before hostPort is even
804	// formed, the colons of an IPv6 literal sit inside the bracket pair the
805	// bracketed-host check already validated (its port is the digits after the
806	// closing ']'), and a number in the base path is past the first path slash
807	// and never reaches hostPort. Ordinary domains, bare IPv4 hosts and
808	// bracketed IPv6 hosts all answer to the same range.
809	//
810	// Only an explicitly written non-empty digit run is judged here: an absent
811	// port and the existing legal "host:" spelling (a colon with an empty port)
812	// stay accepted, and port text that is not all digits keeps its existing
813	// owner — the bracketed-host shape check for a bracketed host, the generic
814	// URL parse error otherwise — so this check never rewords an illegal-port
815	// error that already exists. The check runs in check layer 4
816	// (Config.validate) after the host-shape rules, in routes-array order like
817	// the other field-content checks, so every earlier error keeps its
818	// precedence and one bad route fails the whole read even when a request
819	// would only have hit another, legal route. The reason names the route's
820	// 1-based position, its id and the upstream field and says the port is
821	// outside 0–65535; this is a content error in a syntactically valid JSON
822	// document, never a JSON parse failure. A legal port is never normalized:
823	// the join slices the raw upstream, so "00065535" reaches upstreamURL with
824	// its leading zeros intact.
825	func validateUpstreamPortRange(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
826		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
827			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
828		}
829		port, ok := upstreamExplicitPort(p.hostPort)
830		if !ok || port == "" {
831			return nil
832		}
833		for i := 0; i < len(port); i++ {
834			if port[i] < '0' || port[i] > '9' {
835				// Not a numeric port: the existing illegal-port checks own it.
836				return nil
837			}
838		}
839		if portWithinTCPRange(port) {
840			return nil
841		}
842		return failuref("invalid_config",
843			"%s: upstream port %q is out of range: an explicitly written port must be a decimal number from 0 to 65535 (leading zeros do not change the value); the address is used exactly as configured and the port is never clamped, truncated or rewritten",
844			routeLabel(loc, id), port)
845	}
846	
847	// upstreamExplicitPort slices the explicitly written port out of a hostPort
848	// (the authority after the last '@', per splitUpstream). It reports false
849	// when there is no port separator at all; a present separator with an empty
850	// port ("host:") reports the empty string with true, and the caller leaves
851	// that existing legal spelling alone. The shape decisions of the host

918	// validateBracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's authority for
919	// an IP literal in square brackets: brackets are reserved for an IPv6 (or
920	// future IP-version) literal, so their content must parse as an IPv6 address
921	// — full form, compressed form or an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
922	// tail — and the brackets must wrap the whole host exactly once:
923	//
924	//	"[" IPv6 "]" [ ":" *DIGIT ]
925	//
926	// A port, userinfo and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") are allowed and
927	// never alter the literal's bytes; an empty pair of brackets, a plain
928	// hostname such as "[not-an-ip]", a bare IPv4 address such as
929	// "[127.0.0.1]", a malformed IPv6 literal, a missing closing bracket, a
930	// second bracket group such as "[::1][::2]", a stray closing bracket or any
931	// other text between the closing bracket and the start of the base path
932	// (including junk around the port such as "[::1]:80a" or "[::1]x]:80") are
933	// rejected — a legal first literal never legitimizes trailing content. The
934	// reason names the route, its id and the upstream field. This is a content
935	// error in a syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure,
936	// and the rule is enforced here on the raw bytes rather than left to
937	// url.Parse's parser strictness.
938	func validateBracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
939		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
940			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
941		}
942		hostPort := p.hostPort
943	
944		if !strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
945			return nil // ordinary reg-name (domain) or bare IPv4 host stays as-is
946		}
947		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
948		if !strings.HasPrefix(hostPort, "[") {
949			return failuref("invalid_config",
950				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a single '[' IPv6 address ']' pair: '[' may only open the host", label)
951		}
952		closeBracket := strings.IndexByte(hostPort, ']')
953		if closeBracket < 0 {
954			return failuref("invalid_config",
955				"%s: upstream bracketed host must be a valid IPv6 address but the closing ']' is missing", label)
956		}
957		literal := hostPort[1:closeBracket]
958		// The zone delimiter is percent-encoded in the URL ("%25"); decode the
959		// literal's escapes once so netip sees "fe80::1%eth0" while every other
960		// byte keeps its original spelling.
961		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(literal)
962		if err != nil {
963			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
964		}
965		addr, err := netip.ParseAddr(decoded)
966		if err != nil || !addr.Is6() {
967			// ParseAddr accepts a bare IPv4 address; brackets may only carry
968			// IPv6, so "[127.0.0.1]" is rejected even though it is a valid IP.
969			return invalidBracketedHost(label, literal)
970		}
971		// The one closing bracket ends the host: the rest of the authority may
972		// be empty or the optional port the generic parser already allows
973		// (":" followed by digits, an empty port included). A repeated bracket
974		// group, a stray ']', or any other text before, beside or after a port
975		// fails here even though the first literal was valid — the brackets
976		// must enclose the whole host exactly once.
977		suffix := hostPort[closeBracket+1:]
978		switch {
979		case suffix == "":
980			return nil
981		case strings.ContainsAny(suffix, "[]"):
982			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
983		case suffix[0] != ':':
984			return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
985		}
986		port := suffix[1:]
987		for i := 0; i < len(port); i++ {
988			if port[i] < '0' || port[i] > '9' {
989				return invalidBracketedHostShape(label, suffix)
990			}
991		}
992		return nil
993	}

1002	// validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost checks the split raw upstream's
1003	// authority-without-brackets (hostPort) against the authority grammar:
1004	//
1005	//	host = IP-literal / IPv4address / reg-name
1006	//	IP-literal = "[" ( IPv6address / ... ) "]"
1007	//
1008	// An unbracketed host part may therefore carry at most one colon, the one
1009	// separating the host from its port:
1010	//
1011	//	reg-name [ ":" port ]
1012	//
1013	// Two or more colons are illegal no matter what the bytes spell: a bare IPv6
1014	// literal leaves the host/port boundary undefined (the reader cannot tell
1015	// "::1" from "::1:8080" with a port) and must be written as "[2001:db8::1]",
1016	// while a name such as "api:internal:8080" or even a malformed IPv6-shaped
1017	// spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" is not rescued by a numeric last segment —
1018	// an extra colon stays an extra colon whether or not the address parses as
1019	// IPv6 and whether or not a base path follows. The spelling is rejected on
1020	// the colon count alone: the host and port are never guessed apart, brackets
1021	// are never inserted and a trailing run of digits is never promoted to a
1022	// port, so validity never depends on this Go release's url.Parse port
1023	// strictness.
1024	//
1025	// When the part does parse as an IPv6 literal as written, the reason keeps
1026	// the existing missing-brackets wording; a part that is merely
1027	// multi-colon gets the extra-colon wording. The decision never strips a
1028	// trailing ":<digits>" segment as a hypothetical port: every true bare IPv6
1029	// spelling already parses whole ("::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" are complete
1030	// addresses, whose last hextet merely happens to be digits), so stripping
1031	// would only mislabel a malformed spelling such as "2001:db8:::1" that
1032	// parses once a hextet is removed. Both reasons cover every form — the full
1033	// form, the compressed form ("::1"), an IPv6 address with an embedded IPv4
1034	// tail ("::ffff:192.0.2.1") and a percent-encoded zone ("%25eth0") — and
1035	// both name the route's 1-based position, its id and the upstream field.
1036	//
1037	// Ordinary domains and bare IPv4 hosts (with or without a port) stay
1038	// untouched, and the colons in userinfo or the base path are never
1039	// inspected: only hostPort — the authority after the last '@' and before
1040	// the first '/' according to the shared splitUpstream boundaries — is
1041	// considered. Like the bracketed-host rule this is a content error in a
1042	// syntactically valid JSON document, never a JSON parse failure, and it is
1043	// decided on the raw bytes before url.Parse so the wording cannot regress to
1044	// that parser's generic "invalid port" error.
1045	func validateUnbracketedUpstreamHost(p upstreamParts, loc, id string) *Failure {
1046		if p.schemeEnd < 0 {
1047			return nil // no scheme: the generic absolute-URL check reports this
1048		}
1049		hostPort := p.hostPort
1050		if hostPort == "" || strings.ContainsAny(hostPort, "[]") {
1051			// No host (the generic check reports it) or a bracketed literal,
1052			// which the bracketed-host validator owns.
1053			return nil
1054		}
1055	
1056		// A single colon is the legal host/port separator ("host:8080"); zero
1057		// colons is a bare host. Count raw colons only: percent-encoded colons
1058		// ("%3A") carry no separator byte, and userinfo and the base path were
1059		// sliced off by splitUpstream.
1060		if strings.Count(hostPort, ":") <= 1 {
1061			return nil
1062		}
1063		label := routeLabel(loc, id)
1064	
1065		// Classify the spelling as written, never guessing a host/port split:
1066		// percent-decode once so a "%25eth0" zone reaches netip as "%eth0" while
1067		// every other byte keeps its spelling, then parse the whole hostPort. A
1068		// legal IPv6 literal keeps the existing missing-brackets reason (this
1069		// covers every form, "::1:8080" and "fe80::1:8443" included — a trailing
1070		// hextet of digits is part of the address, not a guessed port); anything
1071		// else that merely carries extra colons gets the extra-colon reason.
1072		decoded, err := url.PathUnescape(hostPort)
1073		if err == nil {
1074			if addr, perr := netip.ParseAddr(decoded); perr == nil && addr.Is6() {
1075				return failuref("invalid_config",
1076					"%s: upstream IPv6 host %q is missing its square brackets: an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in a pair of brackets with any port outside them (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\"); brackets are never added and a trailing number is not guessed as a port",
1077					label, hostPort)
1078			}
1079		}
1080		return failuref("invalid_config",
1081			"%s: upstream %q has an unbracketed host part %q with more than one colon: a host without square brackets may contain at most the one colon separating it from its port (e.g. \"example.com:8080\"); an IPv6 literal must be enclosed in brackets (e.g. \"[2001:db8::1]:8080\") and the host and port are never guessed apart",
1082			label, p.raw, hostPort)
1083	}

1102	// ParseRequest parses and validates one JSON request. Three failure shapes are
1103	// kept apart: a document whose JSON syntax is broken fails as a parse failure
1104	// without guessing a field; a syntactically valid non-object document (array,
1105	// number, string, boolean or null) must be a JSON object; a valid object whose
1106	// method or target is not a string fails on that field, naming the JSON type
1107	// actually received (null counts as a type error, never as a missing field).
1108	// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in the
1109	// object. Only after both fields are present strings are their contents
1110	// (required method, legal token, absolute target without a fragment, a bad
1111	// percent escape, or a direct space/control character) validated, so an empty
1112	// string stays a content error.

1115		if err != nil {
1116			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1117		}
1118		if f := requireJSONObject(body, "invalid_request", "request", false); f != nil {
1119			return nil, f
1120		}
1121	
1122		var rj requestJSON
1123		if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &rj); err != nil {
1124			// The document already parsed as one JSON value and starts with '{';
1125			// keep this as a parse failure rather than a field error if the object
1126			// itself cannot be read.
1127			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "request is not valid JSON: %v", err)
1128		}
1129	
1130		var req Request
1131		// method is always checked before target, regardless of the key order in
1132		// the object; the absent/null/non-string distinction is the shared
1133		// decodeStringField, so only the request wording is added here.
1134		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Method, "method", &req.Method); f != nil {
1135			return nil, f
1136		}
1137		if f := decodeRequestStringField(rj.Target, "target", &req.Target); f != nil {
1138			return nil, f
1139		}
1140	
1141		switch {
1142		case req.Method == "":
1143			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method is required")
1144		case !isToken(req.Method):
1145			return nil, failuref("invalid_request", "method %q is not a legal HTTP method", req.Method)
1146		}

1194	// Resolve matches a validated request against a validated configuration and
1195	// computes the upstream URL. Failure codes are route_not_found and
1196	// route_conflict.
1197	func Resolve(cfg *Config, req *Request) (*Resolution, *Failure) {
1198		// Reject a target carrying a direct space or control character before
1199		// route selection, conflict resolution and query rewriting, so such a
1200		// request can never match a prefix (and carry the byte into
1201		// upstreamURL), report a conflict, or have a remove/set hide the
1202		// offending parameter. ParseRequest already ran this check; it is
1203		// repeated here so a request built in-process cannot bypass it.
1204		if f := validateTargetCharacters(req.Target); f != nil {
1205			return nil, f
1206		}
1207		path := req.Target
1208		if i := strings.IndexByte(path, '?'); i >= 0 {
1209			path = path[:i]
1210		}
1211	
1212		type candidate struct {
1213			route    *Route
1214			concrete bool
1215		}
1216		var matched []candidate
1217		for i := range cfg.Routes {
1218			route := &cfg.Routes[i]
1219			concrete, wildcard := methodMatch(route.Methods, req.Method)
1220			if !concrete && !wildcard {
1221				continue
1222			}
1223			if !prefixMatch(route.PathPrefix, path) {
1224				continue
1225			}
1226			matched = append(matched, candidate{route, concrete})
1227		}
1228		if len(matched) == 0 {
1229			return nil, failuref("route_not_found", "no route matches %s %s", req.Method, path)
1230		}
1231	
1232		// Longest prefix wins.
1233		bestLen := 0
1234		for _, c := range matched {
1235			if n := len(c.route.PathPrefix); n > bestLen {
1236				bestLen = n
1237			}
1238		}
1239		winners := matched[:0]
1240		for _, c := range matched {
1241			if len(c.route.PathPrefix) == bestLen {
1242				winners = append(winners, c)
1243			}
1244		}
1245	
1246		// Among equal prefixes a concrete method beats the wildcard.
1247		var concrete []candidate
1248		for _, c := range winners {
1249			if c.concrete {
1250				concrete = append(concrete, c)
1251			}
1252		}
1253		if len(concrete) > 0 {
1254			winners = concrete
1255		}
1256		if len(winners) > 1 {
1257			ids := make([]string, 0, len(winners))
1258			for _, c := range winners {
1259				ids = append(ids, c.route.ID)
1260			}
1261			sort.Strings(ids)
1262			f := failuref("route_conflict", "multiple routes match %s %s", req.Method, path)
1263			f.Candidates = ids
1264			return nil, f
1265		}
1266	
1267		upstreamURL, f := joinUpstream(winners[0].route, path, req.Target)
1268		if f != nil {
1269			return nil, f
1270		}
1271		return &Resolution{RouteID: winners[0].route.ID, UpstreamURL: upstreamURL}, nil
1272	}

1274	// methodMatch reports whether the method list matches the request method
1275	// concretely (an exact, case-sensitive entry) or via the "*" wildcard.
1276	func methodMatch(methods []string, method string) (concrete, wildcard bool) {
1277		for _, m := range methods {
1278			switch {
1279			case m == "*":
1280				wildcard = true
1281			case m == method:
1282				concrete = true
1283			}
1284		}
1285		return concrete, wildcard
1286	}

1288	// prefixMatch matches raw encoded paths on segment boundaries: "%2F" is never
1289	// treated as a separator and the root prefix matches every origin-path.
1290	func prefixMatch(prefix, path string) bool {
1291		if prefix == "/" {
1292			return true
1293		}
1294		if path == prefix {
1295			return true
1296		}
1297		return strings.HasPrefix(path, prefix) && path[len(prefix)] == '/'

1300	// joinUpstream strips the route prefix from the request path and joins the
1301	// remainder onto the upstream base path with exactly one slash at the
1302	// junction. The junction is one run of literal slashes: every trailing
1303	// slash on the base path and every leading slash on the remainder are
1304	// merged into that single slash, even when either side contributes
1305	// several. Nothing else is normalized: slashes inside either part, the
1306	// remainder's trailing slashes (once non-slash content has appeared),
1307	// ".", ".." and percent escapes such as "%2F" are carried over byte for
1308	// byte, never decoded first. The base path is sliced out of the raw
1309	// upstream so joining never re-encodes, reorders or drops anything
1310	// outside the junction. The raw query is preserved verbatim unless the
1311	// route defines queryTransforms, in which case they rewrite it after
1312	// route selection.
1313	func joinUpstream(route *Route, path, target string) (string, *Failure) {
1314		if _, err := url.Parse(route.Upstream); err != nil {
1315			// Config validation already rejected this.
1316			return "", failuref("invalid_config", "route %q has an invalid upstream: %v", route.ID, err)
1317		}
1318	
1319		var remainder string
1320		switch {
1321		case route.PathPrefix == "/":
1322			// Root keeps the whole following path; "/" itself has an empty remainder.
1323			if path != "/" {
1324				remainder = path
1325			}
1326		default:
1327			remainder = path[len(route.PathPrefix):] // "" or "/...", boundary is a literal slash
1328		}
1329	
1330		// Slice the validated upstream raw so nothing outside the junction is
1331		// normalized or re-escaped. The address boundaries come from the same
1332		// splitUpstream reading the host validators used (scheme://authority
1333		// followed by the base path), so joining can never split userinfo, the
1334		// IPv6 brackets, the port or the base path differently than validation.
1335		parts := splitUpstream(route.Upstream)
1336		basePath := parts.basePath
1337	
1338		// Collapse only the junction run: all trailing slashes of the base
1339		// path meet all leading slashes of the remainder, and the junction
1340		// keeps exactly one slash whether or not anything follows them. A
1341		// remainder made entirely of slashes has no content past the run, so
1342		// it likewise ends in that single slash.
1343		baseTrimmed := strings.TrimRight(basePath, "/")
1344		rest := strings.TrimLeft(remainder, "/")
1345		joined := baseTrimmed + "/" + rest
1346	
1347		result := route.Upstream[:parts.schemeEnd+3] + parts.authority + joined
1348		query, f := applyQueryTransforms(route.QueryTransforms, target)
1349		if f != nil {
1350			return "", f
1351		}
1352		return result + query, nil
1353	}

1355	// firstDirectRawCharacter scans raw path text as written — without decoding
1356	// percent escapes — and returns the first byte that may not appear directly:
1357	// an ASCII space (U+0020), a C0 control byte (U+0000 through U+001F) or DEL

1	// Command saveconfig demonstrates the offline save path of the resolve
2	// configuration: read a config through the fully validating entry point,
3	// save it back to JSON, read the saved document again, and resolve the same
4	// request before and after the save. It runs entirely offline and only uses
5	// the library's public entry points.
6	package main
7	
8	import (
9		"encoding/json"
10		"fmt"
11		"os"
12	
13		"github.com/gzhysuiioo/contractsentinel-audit/contractsentinel"
14	)
15	
16	// configJSON carries a query-rewrite chain: rename every "old" parameter to
17	// "new", then set the (now merged) "new" parameter to the empty string.
18	const configJSON = `{
19	  "routes": [
20	    {
21	      "id": "api",
22	      "methods": ["GET"],
23	      "pathPrefix": "/api",
24	      "upstream": "http://api.internal/v1",
25	      "queryTransforms": [
26	        {"op": "rename", "name": "old", "to": "new"},
27	        {"op": "set", "name": "new", "value": ""}
28	      ]
29	    }
30	  ]
31	}`
32	
33	// requestJSON carries duplicate parameters, an empty value, a raw percent
34	// escape and a parameter without '='.
35	const requestJSON = `{"method":"GET","target":"/api/orders/7?old=1&old=&keep=%2f%41&flag"}`
36	
37	func main() {
38		// 1. Read the configuration through the fully validating entry point.
39		//    ParseConfig runs every check layer; when it returns a Failure there
40		//    is no usable config at all, and the document must not be used.
41		cfg, f := contractsentinel.ParseConfig([]byte(configJSON))
42		if f != nil {
43			fatal(f)
44		}
45	
46		// 2. Save the validated config as JSON. encoding/json drives the
47		//    library's MarshalJSON methods, so routes, methods, prefixes,
48		//    upstreams and the rewrite rules (order and literal strings) are
49		//    preserved; indentation and JSON string escaping may differ from
50		//    the original file.
51		saved, err := json.Marshal(cfg)
52		if err != nil {
53			fatal(&contractsentinel.Failure{Code: "internal_error", Reason: err.Error()})
54		}
55		fmt.Printf("saved config: %s\n", saved)
56	
57		// 3. Re-read the saved document through the same entry point. A
58		//    successful save is not proof the document is a legal config — only
59		//    ParseConfig decides that — so the re-read is validated again, and a
60		//    failure here stops the saved config from being used.
61		reloaded, f := contractsentinel.ParseConfig(saved)
62		if f != nil {
63			fatal(f)
64		}
65	
66		// 4. Resolve the same request against the config from before and after
67		//    the save. Both sides must select the same route and produce the
68		//    same upstreamURL.
69		req, f := contractsentinel.ParseRequest([]byte(requestJSON))
70		if f != nil {
71			fatal(f)
72		}
73		for _, step := range []struct {
74			label string
75			cfg   *contractsentinel.Config
76		}{
77			{"before save", cfg},
78			{"after save ", reloaded},
79		} {
80			res, f := contractsentinel.Resolve(step.cfg, req)
81			if f != nil {
82				fatal(f)
83			}
84			fmt.Printf("%s: routeId=%s upstreamURL=%s\n", step.label, res.RouteID, res.UpstreamURL)
85		}
86	
87		// 5. An empty route list saves as "routes": [] (never null, which the
88		//    reader rejects as a type error), re-reads as a legal config and
89		//    answers every legal request with route_not_found.
90		empty, f := contractsentinel.ParseConfig([]byte(`{"routes": []}`))
91		if f != nil {
92			fatal(f)
93		}
94		savedEmpty, err := json.Marshal(empty)
95		if err != nil {
96			fatal(&contractsentinel.Failure{Code: "internal_error", Reason: err.Error()})
97		}
98		fmt.Printf("saved empty config: %s\n", savedEmpty)
99		reloadedEmpty, f := contractsentinel.ParseConfig(savedEmpty)
100		if f != nil {
101			fatal(f)
102		}
103		if _, f := contractsentinel.Resolve(reloadedEmpty, req); f != nil {
104			fmt.Printf("empty config resolve: code=%s reason=%s\n", f.Code, f.Reason)
105		}
106	}

109	// code and the human-readable reason — and stops; a config or request that
